title: Strabo, Geography 17.1.3–10: the Nile and Alexandria
publisher: LacusCurtius, University of Chicago; H. L. Jones, Loeb translation (1932)
period: Augustan-era account of Egypt and Alexandria, referring also to earlier Ptolemaic history
geography: Alexandria and the Nile valley
summary: Describes Alexandria's harbors, Pharos, streets and royal district, and the importance of Nile inundation, canals and agricultural management.
limitations: Elite literary testimony with Roman imperial sympathies. Descriptive claims and reported numbers are not a population survey, an exact city map or annual household probabilities.

title: Bellum Alexandrinum 1–33: the Alexandrian War
publisher: LacusCurtius, University of Chicago; Loeb translation (1955)
period: Events of 48–47 BCE; authorship traditionally associated with the Caesarian corpus
geography: Alexandria and the Nile Delta
summary: Narrates fighting, barricades, harbor operations and disruption of Caesar's water supply during the Alexandrian War.
limitations: A partisan Roman military narrative with prejudicial descriptions of Alexandrians. It supports a war setting, not invented civilian experiences, precise casualty odds or a claim that the entire Library was destroyed.

title: Chronological Tables for Caesar's Wars (58–45 BCE)
publisher: John T. Ramsey and Kurt A. Raaflaub, Histos 11 (2017); journal page published online 2018
period: 58–45 BCE, including the Alexandrian War of 48–47 BCE
geography: Roman campaigns including Alexandria and Egypt
summary: Reconstructs the sequence of Caesar's campaigns and separates Roman civil-calendar dates from reconstructed Julian dates.
limitations: A scholarly chronology reconstructed from ancient testimony. Day-level dates may be disputed; the game uses year-level anchors and does not reproduce whole tables.

title: Ptolemaic Period
publisher: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities
period: 332–30 BCE; Actium in 31 BCE and the end of Ptolemaic rule in 30 BCE
geography: Egypt, with Alexandria as capital
summary: Provides a heritage-authority overview of Ptolemaic Egypt and the transition following the defeat at Actium.
limitations: A broad public-history overview, not a detailed social dataset. Use the year-level chronology without treating its compressed narrative as proof of every personal consequence.

title: Augustus, Res Gestae, especially section 27
publisher: Livius.org; F. W. Shipley translation from LacusCurtius
period: Augustus's retrospective inscription, completed near the end of his reign in 14 CE
geography: Roman Empire; section 27 concerns annexation of Egypt
summary: Augustus claims to have added Egypt to Roman rule. The inscription offers a contemporary imperial voice for the political transition.
limitations: Self-promotional imperial testimony. It does not describe the response of all Egyptians and must be paired with independent chronology and local evidence.

title: Alexandrian Documents from the Reign of Augustus
publisher: Peter van Minnen, Department of Classics, University of Cincinnati
period: Augustan Alexandria, especially 13 BCE; individual texts and later additions have their own dates
geography: Documents issued in Alexandria, many recovered from reused cartonnage at Abusir el-Melek
summary: Provides scholarly English translations of Alexandrian contracts, letters, petitions and association records, with document identifiers and links to the underlying Greek texts.
limitations: The surviving archive is selective, not representative of every household. Early Roman material is comparative evidence for earlier Ptolemaic years; use each document's actual date.

title: BGU 4.1125.1–15: apprenticeship contract for a musician
publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
period: March/April 13 BCE
geography: Alexandria
summary: Records training in flute playing, the term of apprenticeship, provision of food and clothing, and examination by fellow practitioners.
limitations: The apprentice is enslaved, and this is a specific musical contract. It is evidence for organized training, not universal schooling or the terms of a free child's scribal apprenticeship.

title: BGU 4.1058: wetnursing contract
publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
period: 30 March 13 BCE
geography: Alexandria
summary: Documents paid nursing, infant care and a clause anticipating the possibility of a child's death.
limitations: Both nurse and infant are enslaved in this contract. Its clauses show contemporary concerns; they do not estimate infant mortality or demonstrate that every household employed a wet nurse.

title: BGU 4.1052.1–34: marriage contract
publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
period: 15 April 13 BCE
geography: Alexandria
summary: Records an agreement for a shared life, a dowry and economic and marital obligations.
limitations: One Greek-language legal agreement, with particular status and guardianship conventions. Its terms are not universal Egyptian marriage rules or an observed marriage-age distribution.

title: BGU 4.1141: private letter
publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
period: After 9 April 13 BCE
geography: Alexandria
summary: Preserves correspondence concerning friendship, accusations, work, wages and interpersonal obligations.
limitations: A fragmentary and sometimes difficult personal letter, embedded in unequal relationships. It supports written communication as a theme, not the fictional character's letter or a literacy rate.

title: BGU 4.1117: lease contract for a bakery
publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
period: April/May 13 BCE
geography: Alexandria, Beta quarter
summary: Describes a bakery lease, equipment, rent, repairs and responsibility for taxes, illustrating workshop livelihoods and contractual obligations.
limitations: A single bakery agreement. Monetary amounts and conditions cannot be generalized to all trades or converted directly into the game's abstract wealth score.

title: BGU 4.1151.1–18: partial payment of an inheritance
publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
period: 12 April 13 BCE
geography: Alexandria
summary: Records an agreement concerning the partial payment of an inheritance, supporting a narrative theme of property and obligations between generations.
limitations: A particular legal settlement. It supplies neither a representative inheritance amount nor evidence that all older people held transferable property.

title: Education and Apprenticeship
publisher: Nikolaos Lazaridis (2010), UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology
period: Survey across ancient Egyptian periods, including Ptolemaic and Roman bilingual education
geography: Ancient Egypt; not exclusively Alexandria
summary: Reviews training for scribes and specialist crafts, educational exercises and restricted access to formal schooling.
limitations: A long-period synthesis with uneven evidence. It cannot supply exact Alexandrian enrolment or literacy probabilities, and does not justify giving every child formal schooling.

title: Funerary Rituals (Ptolemaic and Roman Periods)
publisher: Christina Riggs (2010), UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology; University of East Anglia repository
period: Ptolemaic and Roman periods
geography: Egypt; evidence includes Akhmim, Thebes, Tuna el-Gebel and other communities
summary: Surveys burial, commemoration, mourning and funerary associations, including arrangements for members to contribute to funeral costs.
limitations: Rites varied with community, status, resources and religion. Elite mummification evidence is not a universal Alexandrian funeral script; use broad remembrance themes carefully.

title: The abuse of aged parents in the ancient Roman world
publisher: Tim Parkin, Bulletin of the Institute of Classical Studies 66(2), 41–50; online 2024
period: Roman world with Ptolemaic Egyptian petitions of 225 and 221 BCE among the comparative cases
geography: Roman Mediterranean and the Arsinoite nome in Egypt
summary: Examines duties, dependence and care between generations, including papyrus petitions by older parents.
limitations: Sparse, often one-sided dispute evidence from varied times and places. It does not establish rates of neglect or a uniform old-age household arrangement in Alexandria.

title: Volcanic suppression of Nile summer flooding triggers revolt and constrains interstate conflict in ancient Egypt
publisher: Joseph G. Manning and colleagues (2017), Nature Communications 8, 900; author copy at UC Berkeley
period: Ptolemaic Egypt, 305–30 BCE, with later Nilometer measurements used for comparison
geography: Nile basin and Egypt; papyrus survival particularly strong in the Fayyum
summary: Combines environmental reconstructions and ancient writings to examine Nile flood variability, agricultural vulnerability and social stress.
limitations: Ancient flood indications are intermittent and may have dating uncertainty. The continuous Nilometer series begins in 622 CE; this is not a precise annual Alexandrian food-price or famine-risk dataset.

title: Roman Model Life Table (Coale–Demeny Female West Level 3)
publisher: Columbia University / W. V. Harris teaching resources
period: Comparative Roman demographic model; not an observed Ptolemaic cohort
geography: Roman comparison model; not an Alexandria-specific dataset
summary: Provides age-band mortality, survivorship and remaining life expectancy for a model population with life expectancy at birth of 25 years.
limitations: A female model life table, not measured male Alexandrian rates. Converting interval death probabilities into annual hazards assumes within-band timing. Age at death is simulated, not a historical prediction.

title: Quantifying antiquity
publisher: Roger S. Bagnall, Columbia University
period: Contrasts Roman Egyptian census evidence with Hellenistic Egyptian household lists
geography: Egypt, with wider methodological comparisons
summary: Explains the promise and limits of ancient demographic evidence, including why Hellenistic household lists without ages cannot yield life expectancy.
limitations: A methodological essay rather than a downloadable life table. It explicitly cautions against combining Roman and Hellenistic evidence without careful analysis.

title: Life Expectancy
publisher: Sonia Zakrzewski (2015), UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology
period: Long-period review of ancient Egyptian demographic evidence, including Roman model tables
geography: Egypt; evidence from varied populations and sites
summary: Explains demographic methods and biases. Table 1 reproduces a model life table for Roman Egyptian females after Bagnall and Frier (1994), with life expectancy at birth of 22.5 years.
limitations: A later-period female model inferred using census returns and Coale–Demeny West, not observed mortality for a male in Ptolemaic Alexandria. Annual interpolation and the final age-band policy are additional game assumptions; cause-of-death rates are not supplied.

title: Zodiaque de Dendéra (E 13482)
publisher: Musée du Louvre, Egyptian Antiquities collection
period: 50 BCE; catalogue dates the relief to June–August
geography: Hathor temple, Dendera, Upper Egypt
summary: Catalogues a sandstone ceiling relief with zodiacal signs, decans and constellations, providing a contemporary example of Egyptian astral imagery.
limitations: A temple object from Dendera, not an Alexandrian teaching manual. It supplies neither access probabilities nor evidence that astrological predictions were reliable.

title: Alexandrian terracottas
publisher: Vatican Museums, Gregorian Egyptian Museum
period: Ptolemaic and Roman periods
geography: Alexandria; collection objects have varied acquisition histories
summary: Describes Alexandrian figurative terracottas, including mould-made examples and a range of decorative and religious subjects.
limitations: The collection spans multiple periods and some objects entered through the antiquities market. It does not measure workshop employment, wages or apprenticeship access.

title: Statuette of an ancestral king (2003.154)
publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
period: Late Period–Early Ptolemaic Period, 380–246 BCE
geography: Egypt; exact workshop not established in this catalogue entry
summary: Documents a carved wooden ritual figure associated with temple equipment, illustrating skilled Egyptian wood carving.
limitations: Earlier than the player's lifetime and not specifically Alexandrian. The object's interpretation is debated; it does not establish a universal carving curriculum or job ladder.

title: An enigmatic early horoscope: BKT X 29 (P. 11831)
publisher: Berlin Papyrus Database, Egyptian Museum and Papyrus Collection; Marius Gerhardt, Andreas Winkler and Michael Zellmann-Rohrer
period: Late Ptolemaic or early Roman handwriting; astronomical reconstruction best fits 5 June 29 BCE
geography: Egypt; no Alexandrian workshop identified
summary: Examines a Greek horoscope listing astral positions, abbreviations, the ascendant and midheaven, with possible professional or client use.
limitations: The papyrus lacks a personal name and explicit date, and its solar position conflicts with the proposed reconstruction. Its use is uncertain, and no accompanying interpretation survives.

title: Plutarch, Life of Antony 80: Areius and Octavian at Alexandria
publisher: LacusCurtius, University of Chicago; Bernadotte Perrin, Loeb translation
period: Later biography describing the Roman takeover of Alexandria in 30 BCE
geography: Alexandria
summary: Depicts the philosopher Areius receiving public favour from Octavian and interceding for others, illustrating elite intellectual patronage and political access.
limitations: A retrospective literary account, not an administrative record or promotion dataset. It concerns an exceptional elite figure and does not prove ordinary access to Cleopatra's court.

title: Coins in Egypt: Coins of the Ptolemies
publisher: University College London, Digital Egypt for Universities
period: Ptolemaic Egypt, with an overview of earlier coinage
geography: Egypt
summary: Introduces Ptolemaic coin circulation, drachma denominations, bronze and silver coinage, and debt settlement as part of the economy.
limitations: An overview of money and denominations, not an Alexandrian household budget or price series. It does not support the game's prices, wages, asset valuations, fixed returns or a constant currency standard across Roman rule; these remain disclosed gameplay assumptions.

title: LGPN-Egypt: personal names in Egypt
publisher: University of Oxford, Lexicon of Greek Personal Names
period: Current completed coverage: Lower Egypt and the Fayum from the seventh century BCE to 30 BCE; the wider project extends into Roman Egypt
geography: Egypt, with current database coverage focused on Lower Egypt and the Fayum
summary: Introduces a source-based naming database that records personal names alongside attested occupations, dates, family connections and provenance. It supports a varied Greek-language and Egyptian-rendered naming context for fictional characters.
limitations: The game does not reproduce database individuals or claim that every selected name is attested in Alexandria in 66 BCE. Names are not demographic weights, ethnic labels, gender rules or evidence that an occupation belonged to a particular community. Household profiles and event rewards remain authored fiction.

title: Diodorus Siculus, Library of History 1.81.7: childhood learning and livelihood
publisher: LacusCurtius, University of Chicago; C. H. Oldfather, Loeb translation (1933)
period: First-century BCE literary account of Egyptian customs
geography: Egypt generally; not an Alexandrian household survey
summary: Describes children learning livelihood skills from fathers and relatives, alongside limited and uneven access to literacy instruction.
limitations: A generalizing literary account without numerical starting ages. It supports learning and work overlapping in childhood, not the game's exact age gates, wage amounts, universal schooling or an identical experience across households.

title: BGU 4.1124: cancellation of a nailsmith's apprenticeship
publisher: University of Cincinnati, Ancient Alexandria documentary translations
period: After June/July 18 BCE, under early Roman rule
geography: Alexandria
summary: Records Hermaiskos, a son not yet of age, being trained in nailsmithing; cancelling the agreement permits his father to place him with another master.
limitations: The apprentice's numerical age is unstated. The document postdates the cohort's Ptolemaic childhood and does not establish age 12 as a norm, free access to an apprenticeship or the game's pay and skill gains.

title: BGU 4.1151.2: Loan agreement
publisher: University of Cincinnati; Peter van Minnen translation
period: 12 April 13 BCE, early Roman period
geography: Alexandria
summary: Records a money loan with scheduled instalments, default penalties and enforcement claims against debtors and workshop property.
limitations: One early Roman contract, later than the Ptolemaic beginning of the game. Contractual enforcement clauses do not establish how frequently they were exercised or support violent collectors, murder, or the game's loan terms and risks.

title: The Ptolemaic Period (332–30 BCE)
publisher: Brian Muhs (2016); The Ancient Egyptian Economy: 3000–30 BCE, Cambridge University Press; pp. 211–252; DOI 10.1017/CBO9781316286364.008
period: Ptolemaic Egypt, 332–30 BCE; individual examples have earlier dates
geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
summary: Contracts, witnesses, registration, informal trust and varied exchange networks. Read scope: Relevant full-text sections, especially pp.227–230,236–238,246–247.
limitations: Egypt-wide synthesis with earlier and provincial examples; does not establish exact Alexandrian prices, wages or access rules for this cohort. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

title: Introduction
publisher: Nico Dogaer (2026); Industry, Trade and the State in Ptolemaic Egypt, Cambridge University Press; pp. 1–20; DOI 10.1017/9781009413411.005
period: Ptolemaic Egypt; institutional discussion across the period
geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
summary: Sector-specific state intervention alongside private activity and local networks. Read scope: Publisher abstract and authorized excerpt pp.1–10; not the full book.
limitations: Institutional framework, not a dossier of one Alexandrian business or proof of unrestricted modern entrepreneurship. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

title: Family Affairs: Guild Regulations and Family Relationships in Roman Egypt
publisher: Philip F. Venticinque (2010); Greek, Roman, and Byzantine Studies 50(2); pp. 273–294
period: Roman Egypt; near-cohort examples from 14–37 CE and 16 CE, with many later comparisons
geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
summary: Overlap of household, business, apprenticeship and mutual-support relationships. Read scope: Relevant full-text sections pp.277–283,288–292.
limitations: Chiefly provincial Roman Egypt; cases from43CE,47CE and later are outside the cohort. Earlier comparative cases do not establish Alexandrian guild rules. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

title: Music and Musicians
publisher: Sibylle Emerit (2013); UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology 1(1)
period: Long-period Egyptian survey; examples must retain their own dates
geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
summary: Instrument specialization, hired performers, private and religious settings, patron relationships. Read scope: Relevant full-text sections, printed pp.4–5,7–11.
limitations: Long chronological survey. Many details concern earlier periods or later Roman examples; no universal local training ladder or wage schedule follows. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

title: Temple Festivals of the Ptolemaic and Roman Periods
publisher: Filip Coppens (2009); UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology 1(1)
period: Ptolemaic and Roman periods; chiefly Upper Egyptian temple evidence
geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
summary: Festival preparation, public processions, travel and distinctions between public and restricted participation. Read scope: Substantive full article, printed pp.1–8.
limitations: Detailed cases are chiefly Upper Egyptian; named Edfu/Dendara festivals must not be relocated into Alexandria. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

title: World travellers: the associations of Artists of Dionysus
publisher: Sophia Aneziri (2009); Wandering Poets in Ancient Greek Culture: Travel, Locality and Pan-Hellenism, Cambridge University Press; pp. 217–236; DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511576133.009
period: Hellenistic professional performance networks in the wider Greek world
geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
summary: Professional performance, festival networks and travel as relevant themes. Read scope: Publisher summary and metadata only.
limitations: Mediterranean-wide comparison; does not verify a particular Alexandrian association or its admissions in66BCE. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

title: A Note on στεφάνων καθαίρεσις in the Newly Published Papyrus on the Theadelpheia Festival
publisher: Lucia Prauscello (2023); Zeitschrift für Papyrologie und Epigraphik 226; pp. 99–106
period: Alexandrian programme probably from 242 BCE, earlier than the game cohort
geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
summary: Alexandrian festival organization, venues, sponsorship and practical coordination. Read scope: Relevant full-text sections pp.99–100,102,104–105 and conclusion.
limitations: Programme probably belongs to242BCE, an earlier precedent. Crown-handling interpretations remain disputed; no literal event recreation for this cohort. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

title: A Late First Century BC Greek Astronomical Almanac: P.Petrie Mus. astr.
publisher: Gaia Fanelli, Alexander Jones (2019); Zeitschrift für Papyrologie und Epigraphik 212; pp. 199–213
period: Late first century BCE, reconstructed late-Augustan astronomical work
geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
summary: Calculated planetary tables, copying and consultation; probable use as horoscope inputs. Read scope: Introduction pp.199–200 and commentary/reconstruction pp.205–213; no independent collation of fragment readings.
limitations: Provenance unknown. Reconstructed late-Augustan dates fall late in the cohort; appropriate for optional later work, not the sole first accomplishment or proof of Alexandrian employment. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

title: Parapēgmata and poleis: astrometeorological calendars in the Hellenistic city
publisher: Ruben Post (2025); The Journal of Hellenic Studies 145; pp. 1–21; DOI 10.1017/S0075426925100293
period: Hellenistic city calendars, including earlier Egyptian comparative material
geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
summary: Hellenistic calendar compilation and discussion of observation, regional applicability and unreliable forecasts. Read scope: Abstract and relevant full-text sections pp.1–4,6–8.
limitations: Broad Hellenistic evidence; Egyptian P.Hib.27 is earlier and no specific Alexandrian occupation is established. Weather lore is not validated prediction. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

title: Pythagoreanising Aristotle: Eudorus and the systematisation of Platonism
publisher: Mauro Bonazzi (2013); Aristotle, Plato and Pythagoreanism in the First Century BC: New Directions for Philosophy, Cambridge University Press; pp. 160–186; DOI 10.1017/CBO9781139096713.010
period: First-century BCE Alexandrian philosophical interpretation
geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
summary: First-centuryBCE Alexandrian philosophical argument and competing interpretations. Read scope: Author institutional abstract and publisher metadata only.
limitations: Intellectual study, not evidence for universal schooling, ordinary teaching wages or easy access to elite patronage. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

title: Egyptian Warriors: The Machimoi of Herodotus and the Ptolemaic Army
publisher: Christelle Fischer-Bovet (2013); The Classical Quarterly 63(1); pp. 209–236; DOI 10.1017/S000983881200064X
period: Ptolemaic military participation with earlier literary comparisons
geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
summary: Reassessment of Egyptian military participation and simplistic inherited ethnic/status categories. Read scope: Publisher extract and bibliographic metadata only.
limitations: Does not establish unrestricted enlistment, promotion chances or a specific cohort member's military career. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

title: Ptolemaic Berenike: Resources, Logistics, and Daily Life in a Hellenistic Fortress on the Red Sea Coast of Egypt
publisher: Marek A. Woźniak, Steven E. Sidebotham, Marta Osypińska, Alfredo Carannante, Joanna K. Rądkowska (2021); American Journal of Archaeology 125(2); pp. 247–281; DOI 10.3764/aja.125.2.0247
period: Ptolemaic Berenike, a Red Sea port and fortress
geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
summary: Connections between ports, supply, water, military needs and civilian activity. Read scope: Abstract and introduction/methods/geographical sections pp.247–251.
limitations: Berenike is on the Red Sea, not Alexandria. These networks inspire authored voyage-linked stories; a new playable location is not implied. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.
